clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder caused by biallelic L2HGDH mutations, encoding the mitochondrial FAD-dependent L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase.

Brain MRI is often diagnostic: a subcortical (peripheral-to-central) leukoencephalopathy with symmetrical involvement of the dentate nuclei, globus pallidus, putamen and caudate, plus cerebellar atrophy.
Slowly progressive childhood-onset disease with developmental delay, cerebellar ataxia, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, epilepsy, macrocephaly and cognitive decline.
There is a markedly increased lifetime risk of brain tumours (malignant gliomas, medulloblastoma, primitive neuroectodermal tumours), so surveillance imaging matters.
Urine organic acids show raised 2-hydroxyglutarate; chiral separation confirms the L-enantiomer and excludes the D and combined forms.
L-2-hydroxyglutarate is a metabolite-repair substrate that, when it accumulates, acts as an oncometabolite inhibiting alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases.
Riboflavin and FAD supplementation have been tried given the FAD-dependent enzyme, but benefit is unproven; genetic confirmation is by L2HGDH sequencing.
reference.pathophysiology: L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in L2HGDH, which encodes L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial FAD-linked enzyme that oxidises L-2-hydroxyglutarate back to 2-oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate). L-2-hydroxyglutarate arises as an error metabolite when malate dehydrogenase and related dehydrogenases act on alpha-ketoglutarate, and L2HGDH normally repairs this by reconverting it. Loss of the enzyme leads to accumulation of L-2-hydroxyglutarate in plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, urine and brain. Like its D-enantiomer, L-2-hydroxyglutarate competitively inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, including histone and DNA demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases, disturbing epigenetic and metabolic regulation; this underlies the characteristic leukoencephalopathy and the predisposition to malignant brain tumours.
additionalDifferentials: Other leukoencephalopathies (e.g. Canavan disease, vanishing white matter disease)
Glutaric aciduria type I (macrocephaly with basal ganglia change)
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acid analysis with chiral separation
Brain MRI focused on subcortical white matter, dentate nuclei and basal ganglia
redFlags: New focal neurological deficit or rapidly progressive symptoms suggesting a brain tumour
reference.prognosis: The disorder is slowly progressive over years to decades with variable disability, and many patients survive into adulthood. The principal serious complication is the substantially increased risk of malignant brain tumours; no curative treatment is available.
pitfalls: Not performing chiral separation, leading to misclassification of the enantiomer.
Missing the elevated brain-tumour risk and omitting surveillance imaging.
Mistaking the leukoencephalopathy for an acquired demyelinating disorder.
Attributing macrocephaly and basal ganglia signal change solely to glutaric aciduria type I.
management: Offer supportive symptomatic care as no curative treatment exists, with a trial of riboflavin given the FAD-dependent nature of the deficient enzyme
Control seizures with appropriate antiseizure medication
Manage cerebellar ataxia, spasticity and extrapyramidal features with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and antispasticity measures
Undertake regular surveillance neuroimaging because of the markedly increased lifetime risk of malignant brain tumours
Provide developmental, educational and multidisciplinary support for cognitive decline and disability
Offer genetic counselling and testing of at-risk relatives given autosomal recessive inheritance
Escalate to neuro-oncology promptly if surveillance imaging or new focal signs suggest tumour development
